articles.title: Did the Quran Move Haman From Persia to Egypt?
articles.excerpt: Critics say the Quran borrowed Haman from the Book of Esther and placed him in Pharaoh's court by mistake. The charge rests on assumptions worth testing.
articles.content:
The Quran names a man called Haman as an official in the court of the Pharaoh who opposed Moses. The Hebrew Bible knows a Haman too, but he appears in the Book of Esther as a minister of the Persian king, roughly a thousand years after Moses. Critics conclude that the Quran confused two stories and moved a Persian villain into Egypt. The charge of anachronism is serious and deserves a careful hearing, which means examining what it assumes as well as what it asserts.

[ce_figure id="pexels-29390088"]Explore the majestic Pyramids of Giza under a sunny sky with distant travelers on camels.[/ce_figure]

What the Quran says about Haman

Haman appears six times in the Quran, always alongside Pharaoh. He is named with Pharaoh and their armies as those who feared the Israelites, as a builder whom Pharaoh orders to raise a tower, and among the arrogant who were destroyed.

وَنُمَكِّنَ لَهُمْ فِى ٱلْأَرْضِ وَنُرِىَ فِرْعَوْنَ وَهَٰمَٰنَ وَجُنُودَهُمَا مِنْهُم مَّا كَانُوا۟ يَحْذَرُونَ ﴿٦﴾
"And establish them in the land and show Pharaoh and [his minister] Haman and their soldiers through them that which they had feared."
Sūrat al-Qaṣaṣ 28:6

The fullest passage is the tower episode. Pharaoh mocks the idea of a God above and orders Haman to build something high enough to look at the God of Moses.

وَقَالَ فِرْعَوْنُ يَٰٓأَيُّهَا ٱلْمَلَأُ مَا عَلِمْتُ لَكُم مِّنْ إِلَٰهٍ غَيْرِى فَأَوْقِدْ لِى يَٰهَٰمَٰنُ عَلَى ٱلطِّينِ فَٱجْعَل لِّى صَرْحًۭا لَّعَلِّىٓ أَطَّلِعُ إِلَىٰٓ إِلَٰهِ مُوسَىٰ وَإِنِّى لَأَظُنُّهُۥ مِنَ ٱلْكَٰذِبِينَ ﴿٣٨﴾
"And Pharaoh said, "O eminent ones, I have not known you to have a god other than me. Then ignite for me, O Haman, [a fire] upon the clay and make for me a tower that I may look at the God of Moses. And indeed, I do think he is among the liars.""
Sūrat al-Qaṣaṣ 28:38
وَقَالَ فِرْعَوْنُ يَٰهَٰمَٰنُ ٱبْنِ لِى صَرْحًۭا لَّعَلِّىٓ أَبْلُغُ ٱلْأَسْبَٰبَ ﴿٣٦﴾ أَسْبَٰبَ ٱلسَّمَٰوَٰتِ فَأَطَّلِعَ إِلَىٰٓ إِلَٰهِ مُوسَىٰ وَإِنِّى لَأَظُنُّهُۥ كَٰذِبًۭا ۚ وَكَذَٰلِكَ زُيِّنَ لِفِرْعَوْنَ سُوٓءُ عَمَلِهِۦ وَصُدَّ عَنِ ٱلسَّبِيلِ ۚ وَمَا كَيْدُ فِرْعَوْنَ إِلَّا فِى تَبَابٍۢ ﴿٣٧﴾
"And Pharaoh said, "O Haman, construct for me a tower that I might reach the ways - The ways into the heavens - so that I may look at the deity of Moses; but indeed, I think he is a liar." And thus was made attractive to Pharaoh the evil of his deed, and he was averted from the [right] way. And the plan of Pharaoh was not except in ruin."
Sūrat Ghāfir 40:36 to 37

Three features stand out. Haman is a court official with authority over construction. He fires clay to make bricks. He is linked to Pharaoh and to Qarun (Korah), and the Quran treats all three as figures of the Egyptian period. Nothing in these verses resembles the Haman of Esther, who is a Persian vizier at Susa, plots the destruction of the Jews, and dies on the gallows he prepared for Mordecai.

The argument from borrowing

The critic's case runs in three steps. The only Haman known to ancient literature is the one in Esther. The Quran mentions a Haman. Therefore the Quran took the name from Esther and placed it in the wrong century. The conclusion depends on the first premise, and the first premise is an argument from silence.

The Book of Exodus does not name a single official at Pharaoh's court. It does not even name the Pharaoh. Its narrative concerns Moses, Aaron and the king, and the officials around the king remain anonymous. Egyptian royal administration employed overseers of works, chief builders and quarry masters by the hundred, and the names of most of them are lost. To argue that the Quran cannot name an Egyptian official because the Bible does not name him is to treat the Bible as a complete register of Egyptian personnel, which it never claims to be.

The borrowing argument also has to explain why the borrowing left no trace of its source. If a seventh-century author wished to decorate the Moses story with a famous villain from Esther, the obvious features to carry over would be the ones that made Haman famous: the plot against the Jews, Mordecai, Esther herself, the king of Persia, the feast of Purim. The Quran carries over none of them. What remains is a name and nothing else, attached to a role (overseer of building in brick) that has no parallel in Esther at all.

[ce_figure id="pexels-14145503"]High angle view of an ancient mud-brick village showcasing traditional architecture.[/ce_figure]

The Egyptian name question

Some Muslim writers have gone further and claimed that Egyptology has confirmed a Haman in the records of the New Kingdom. The most widely circulated version comes from the French physician Maurice Bucaille, who reported that an entry in Hermann Ranke's dictionary of Egyptian personal names matched the Quranic Haman and gave his profession as chief of the workers in the stone quarries.

That claim should be handled with caution, and this site does not rely on it. Critics who checked Ranke's entry point out that the name is incompletely read, that the title belongs to a different source, and that the person in question served the temple of Amun at a date that does not fit the Exodus on standard chronologies. Whatever one concludes about that particular inscription, an apologetic built on a disputed reading of a single entry is weaker than the simpler point it was meant to support. The defence of the Quran here does not need Bucaille.

The simpler point is this. Names recur. The Hebrew Bible itself has several men named Nathan, Zechariah and Joseph in different centuries and places, and nobody accuses the biblical authors of anachronism for it. A Persian official named Haman and an Egyptian official with a name rendered in Arabic as Haman can both exist without either depending on the other. The critic must show that the Quranic Haman is the Esther Haman, and the only evidence offered is the shared name.

[ce_figure id="pexels-39617543"]Majestic ancient Egyptian columns in weathered stone under clear sky.[/ce_figure]

The tower and the bricks

Critics add a second charge: the tower episode borrows from the Tower of Babel in Genesis 11, which was built in Mesopotamia. The Quran, they say, has merged Babel, Esther and Exodus into one confused scene.

Read on its own terms, the Quranic scene is a piece of royal mockery. Pharaoh, who claims to know no god but himself, orders a high structure so that he can look for the God of Moses, adding that he thinks Moses a liar. The point is his arrogance, and the Quran says so directly: his evil deed was made attractive to him.

The building material is fired clay brick, which matches Egyptian practice; mud brick, fired or sun-dried, was the ordinary material of Egyptian construction outside the great stone monuments, and Exodus itself describes the Israelites making bricks for Pharaoh. A king ordering his master of works to build high is no more a borrowing from Babel than any other story about a tall building.

What an honest conclusion looks like

The anachronism charge would succeed if three things were true: that the Bible preserves the names of all of Pharaoh's officials, that only one Haman could ever have existed in the ancient Near East, and that the Quran's Haman shares the identifying features of the Haman in Esther. None of the three holds. The Bible names none of the officials, names recur across cultures, and the Quranic Haman shares nothing with the Persian Haman beyond the name.

What remains is a figure who is otherwise unattested in surviving records. That is a real limitation, and it is the same limitation that applies to most named individuals in ancient religious narratives, including many in the Bible. Absence from the surviving record is a reason for humility on both sides. It falls well short of proof that the Quran made a mistake, and the specific theory of borrowing from Esther fits the evidence poorly.

The reader who wants to test the Quran's historical claims will find stronger ground elsewhere: in how the text was preserved, in its account of earlier scripture, and in the specific historical details it gives about the Prophet's own time. On Haman, the honest verdict is that the critic has not carried the burden of proof.

articles.title: Is Allah a Moon God, or the God of Abraham?
articles.excerpt: A popular claim says Allah began as an Arabian moon god or the idol Hubal. The evidence points the other way, and the Quran answers the charge itself.
articles.content:
A claim circulates widely in Christian polemic: Allah was originally a pagan Arabian deity, perhaps a moon god, perhaps the idol Hubal who stood in the Kaaba, and Muhammad simply promoted him to supreme status. The crescent on mosque domes is offered as the proof. The argument has been repeated so often that many people assume scholars accept it. They do not, and the reasons are worth setting out, along with the stronger question that lies behind the slogan.

[ce_figure id="pexels-16500828"]A image of a crescent moon set against a deep black sky, showcasing its serene beauty.[/ce_figure]

The word Allah

Allah is the Arabic word for God, formed from the definite article and the word for a deity, cognate with the Hebrew El and Eloah and the Aramaic Alaha. Arabic-speaking Christians and Jews used it before Islam and use it today. An Arabic Bible opens with the words "In the beginning God created the heavens and the earth" using Allah for God, and Arab Christians pray to Allah in their churches every Sunday. Whatever the word meant to pagan Arabs, it was the ordinary Semitic term for the one God among monotheists who spoke the language.

The more careful Christian critics concede this point. Their stronger argument is theological: granted that Allah is a generic word, do Muslims and Christians mean the same being by it? That is a fair question, and it is answered at the end of this article. The moon god thesis is a different claim, and it fails on its own evidence.

What the Quran says the pagans believed

The Quran reports that the Meccan polytheists already acknowledged Allah as the creator of the heavens and the earth. Their error, as the Quran describes it, lay in associating partners with Him: lesser deities, intercessors and daughters.

وَلَئِن سَأَلْتَهُم مَّنْ خَلَقَ ٱلسَّمَٰوَٰتِ وَٱلْأَرْضَ وَسَخَّرَ ٱلشَّمْسَ وَٱلْقَمَرَ لَيَقُولُنَّ ٱللَّهُ ۖ فَأَنَّىٰ يُؤْفَكُونَ ﴿٦١﴾
"If you asked them, "Who created the heavens and earth and subjected the sun and the moon?" they would surely say, "Allah." Then how are they deluded?"
Sūrat al-ʿAnkabūt 29:61

The goddesses they worshipped are named, and the Quran rejects them outright.

أَفَرَءَيْتُمُ ٱللَّٰتَ وَٱلْعُزَّىٰ ﴿١٩﴾ إِنْ هِىَ إِلَّآ أَسْمَآءٌۭ سَمَّيْتُمُوهَآ أَنتُمْ وَءَابَآؤُكُم مَّآ أَنزَلَ ٱللَّهُ بِهَا مِن سُلْطَٰنٍ ۚ إِن يَتَّبِعُونَ إِلَّا ٱلظَّنَّ وَمَا تَهْوَى ٱلْأَنفُسُ ۖ وَلَقَدْ جَآءَهُم مِّن رَّبِّهِمُ ٱلْهُدَىٰٓ ﴿٢٣﴾
"So have you considered al-Lat and al-'Uzza? They are not but [mere] names you have named them - you and your forefathers - for which Allah has sent down no authority. They follow not except assumption and what [their] souls desire, and there has already come to them from their Lord guidance."
Sūrat al-Najm 53:19 to 23

This is the opposite of what the moon god thesis requires. If Muhammad had elevated a pagan deity, the Quran would be expected to keep that deity's associations, consort or symbols. It does the reverse. It takes the one name the polytheists already recognised as the highest and strips away every partner, daughter and image attached to it. The three most prominent goddesses of the Hijaz are dismissed as names without authority. The Prophet's message, in the Quran's own framing, was a return to the faith of Abraham, which the Meccans claimed to honour and had corrupted.

[ce_figure id="pexels-28141977"]A night view of the Blue Mosque in Istanbul, showcasing its stunning architecture and illuminated domes.[/ce_figure]

Hubal and the Kaaba

The early historians report that an idol of Hubal stood inside the Kaaba before Islam and that the Meccans consulted divining arrows before it. The same historians report that when the Prophet entered Mecca in 630, the idols in and around the Kaaba were destroyed, Hubal among them. A prophet who wished to honour Hubal under another name would hardly order his statue broken. The early sources consistently present Hubal as one of the partners whose worship Islam abolished.

Pre-Islamic poetry and inscriptions also distinguish Allah from Hubal. Pagan Arabs could swear by Allah and by their other gods in the same breath, which shows they regarded them as different beings. The Quran's demand was that they keep the first and abandon the rest.

[ce_figure id="pexels-8357639"]Majestic night sky over sand dunes in Morocco's Zagora Province, highlighting the beauty of nature's tranquility.[/ce_figure]

The crescent and the moon

The moon god thesis was popularised in the twentieth century by writers who drew on older archaeological work on South Arabian religion, where a moon deity was worshipped under names such as Almaqah, Sin and Wadd. None of those names is Allah, and the inscriptions come from Yemen and its neighbours, far from Mecca. Scholars of pre-Islamic Arabia do not accept the step from "some Arabians worshipped a moon god" to "Allah was a moon god." It has no textual support.

The crescent symbol confirms nothing. It is absent from the Quran and from the Prophet's practice. It became a common emblem of Muslim states much later, largely through Ottoman usage, and it has no doctrinal status. The Quran treats the moon as a created sign and forbids its worship in so many words:

وَمِنْ ءَايَٰتِهِ ٱلَّيْلُ وَٱلنَّهَارُ وَٱلشَّمْسُ وَٱلْقَمَرُ ۚ لَا تَسْجُدُوا۟ لِلشَّمْسِ وَلَا لِلْقَمَرِ وَٱسْجُدُوا۟ لِلَّهِ ٱلَّذِى خَلَقَهُنَّ إِن كُنتُمْ إِيَّاهُ تَعْبُدُونَ ﴿٣٧﴾
"And of His signs are the night and day and the sun and moon. Do not prostrate to the sun or to the moon, but prostrate to Allah, who created them, if it should be Him that you worship."
Sūrat Fuṣṣilat 41:37

A scripture that forbids prostration to the moon is a poor candidate for a moon cult in disguise.

The real question: the same God?

The serious version of the objection grants all of the above and asks whether the God described in the Quran is the God of the Bible. The Quran's answer is direct. It instructs Muslims to tell the Jews and Christians that their God is one:

۞ وَلَا تُجَٰدِلُوٓا۟ أَهْلَ ٱلْكِتَٰبِ إِلَّا بِٱلَّتِى هِىَ أَحْسَنُ إِلَّا ٱلَّذِينَ ظَلَمُوا۟ مِنْهُمْ ۖ وَقُولُوٓا۟ ءَامَنَّا بِٱلَّذِىٓ أُنزِلَ إِلَيْنَا وَأُنزِلَ إِلَيْكُمْ وَإِلَٰهُنَا وَإِلَٰهُكُمْ وَٰحِدٌۭ وَنَحْنُ لَهُۥ مُسْلِمُونَ ﴿٤٦﴾
"And do not argue with the People of the Scripture except in a way that is best, except for those who commit injustice among them, and say, "We believe in that which has been revealed to us and revealed to you. And our God and your God is one; and we are Muslims [in submission] to Him.""
Sūrat al-ʿAnkabūt 29:46

From the Quran's side, then, the identity of reference is affirmed: the God who spoke to Abraham, Moses and Jesus is the God who speaks in the Quran. The disagreement concerns what is true of Him. Christians confess God as Trinity and Jesus as God incarnate; the Quran denies both and describes God this way:

بِسْمِ ٱللَّهِ ٱلرَّحْمَٰنِ ٱلرَّحِيمِ قُلْ هُوَ ٱللَّهُ أَحَدٌ ﴿١﴾ وَلَمْ يَكُن لَّهُۥ كُفُوًا أَحَدٌۢ ﴿٤﴾
"Say, "He is Allah, [who is] One, Nor is there to Him any equivalent.""
Sūrat al-Ikhlāṣ 112:1 to 4

A disagreement about a person's attributes presupposes that both parties are talking about the same person. Jews reject the Trinity and the divinity of Jesus as firmly as Muslims do, and Christians do not generally say that the Jews worship a moon god or a different deity; they say the Jews have an incomplete or mistaken understanding of the one God. The same reasoning applies to Muslims. One may think the Quran describes God wrongly, which is the substance of the Christian objection, without pretending that Muslims bow to an idol. The theological dispute is real and worth having on its merits. The moon god story is a distraction from it.

articles.title: Was Muhammad Possessed? The First Revelation and the Pause
articles.excerpt: The first revelation left Muhammad shaken, and one report speaks of despair during a pause. Critics read possession into it. The sources say otherwise.
articles.content:
The earliest account of the first revelation in Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī does not flatter its subject. Muhammad returns from the cave of Hira trembling, asks to be wrapped in a cloak and tells his wife that he fears for himself. In another version a later narrator adds that, during a pause in revelation, he grieved so deeply that he went to mountain tops intending to throw himself down. Critics argue that a true prophet would not react this way, and some conclude that his experience was demonic. The sources deserve a closer reading than the charge gives them.

[ce_figure id="pexels-28593362"]Explore the stunning rock formations inside a cave in New Athos, Abkhazia.[/ce_figure]

What the earliest account says

ʿĀʾishah's narration, transmitted by ʿUrwah ibn al-Zubayr and al-Zuhrī, opens the collection. It describes true dreams, a love of seclusion, worship in the cave of Hira, and then the sudden arrival of the angel, who commands him to recite. He answers that he cannot, is pressed three times, and receives the opening verses of Sūrat al-ʿAlaq.

بِسْمِ ٱللَّهِ ٱلرَّحْمَٰنِ ٱلرَّحِيمِ ٱقْرَأْ بِٱسْمِ رَبِّكَ ٱلَّذِى خَلَقَ ﴿١﴾ عَلَّمَ ٱلْإِنسَٰنَ مَا لَمْ يَعْلَمْ ﴿٥﴾
"Recite in the name of your Lord who created - Taught man that which he knew not."
Sūrat al-ʿAlaq 96:1 to 5

He returns home shaking and asks Khadījah to cover him. When the fear passes he tells her what happened. Her answer is the first assessment of his experience by anyone who knew him well:

لَقَدْ خَشِيتُ عَلَى نَفْسِي. فَقَالَتْ خَدِيجَةُ كَلاَّ وَاللَّهِ مَا يُخْزِيكَ اللَّهُ أَبَدًا، إِنَّكَ لَتَصِلُ الرَّحِمَ، وَتَحْمِلُ الْكَلَّ
""I fear for myself." Khadijah said: "Never. By God, God will never disgrace you. You keep ties with your kin and you bear the burdens of the weak.""
Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī 3

She then takes him to her cousin Waraqah ibn Nawfal, a Christian who knew the earlier scriptures, and Waraqah identifies the visitor as the same angelic messenger who came to Moses. The report records fear, and it records the people closest to him interpreting the event, from the start, as revelation from God.

Is fear the mark of a false prophet?

The critic's first premise is that a genuine encounter with God produces peace, so terror is a warning sign. The biblical record does not support that premise. When Isaiah sees the Lord in the temple, his first words are a cry of ruin: he is a man of unclean lips who has seen the King.

Daniel, after his vision by the Tigris, loses his strength and falls into a deep sleep with his face to the ground. Moses hides his face at the burning bush because he is afraid to look at God. Jeremiah protests that he is only a child and cannot speak. In the scriptures that critics themselves accept, the first contact with the divine overwhelms the human being who receives it.

Measured against that pattern, Muhammad's reaction is what one would expect from a man who did not seek prophethood and did not anticipate it. A fabricator inventing a call to prophecy has every reason to make the scene confident and triumphant. The early Muslim community preserved a version in which the Prophet is frightened and doubts himself. That is an embarrassing detail, and historians generally treat embarrassing details in a tradition as more likely to be authentic, precisely because no one would invent them.

The despair report and its chain

The sharpest form of the charge rests on the passage about the mountains. It appears in Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī 6982, after ʿĀʾishah's account ends with Waraqah's death and the pause in revelation. The Arabic contains a phrase that the English translations often blur:

حَتَّى حَزِنَ النَّبِيُّ صلى الله عليه وسلم فِيمَا بَلَغَنَا حُزْنًا غَدَا مِنْهُ مِرَارًا كَىْ يَتَرَدَّى مِنْ رُءُوسِ شَوَاهِقِ الْجِبَالِ
"until the Prophet grieved, according to what has reached us, with a grief that sent him out repeatedly intending to throw himself from the tops of high mountains"
Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī 6982

The words fīmā balaghanā, "according to what has reached us," belong to al-Zuhrī. They mark the sentence as something he heard without naming his source, which hadith scholars call a balāgh: a report with a broken chain. Ibn Ḥajar al-ʿAsqalānī, the principal commentator on al-Bukhārī, made this point in his commentary: the mountain passage is al-Zuhrī's addition and is not part of ʿĀʾishah's connected narration. Al-Bukhārī placed it where he did as supplementary material, and his own version of the account at the opening of the collection omits it entirely.

This matters for the argument. A connected report from ʿĀʾishah meets al-Bukhārī's standard of authenticity. An unattributed remark from a narrator born decades after the event does not. The critic who presents the despair passage as the testimony of Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī is presenting the weakest sentence in the report as if it carried the authority of the strongest.

Even granting the report, it describes grief at the loss of contact with God, and each time, it says, Gabriel appeared and told him that he was truly God's messenger. The narrative's own point is that the pause tested him and that God answered. Despair at divine silence is a theme the Psalms know well. Elijah, after his victory on Mount Carmel, sat under a tree and asked to die. Nobody concludes from that passage that Elijah was possessed.

[ce_figure id="pexels-28263982"]Sunset view over evergreen trees and rocky landscape in Idaho Springs, Colorado.[/ce_figure]

The charge of madness in the Quran

The accusation that Muhammad was mad or possessed is older than his modern critics. His Meccan opponents made it, and the Quran records and answers it.

مَآ أَنتَ بِنِعْمَةِ رَبِّكَ بِمَجْنُونٍۢ ﴿٢﴾
"You are not, [O Muhammad], by the favor of your Lord, a madman."
Sūrat al-Qalam 68:2
وَمَا صَاحِبُكُم بِمَجْنُونٍۢ ﴿٢٢﴾
"And your companion is not [at all] mad."
Sūrat al-Takwīr 81:22

The Arabs of his day had clear categories for inspired speech that did not come from God: the kāhin (soothsayer), who spoke in short rhymed oracles for a fee; the majnūn (one touched by jinn); and the shāʿir (poet), whose verse was believed to come from a familiar spirit. The Quran rejects each label by name, and its content sits awkwardly with all of them. Soothsayers told fortunes and found lost camels. The Quran demands the worship of one God, forbids the practices on which soothsayers lived, condemns the idols of the Prophet's own tribe and orders justice to orphans and the poor. A spirit seeking to lead people away from God has chosen a strange message to deliver.

[ce_figure id="pexels-38606209"]Expansive view of a rugged mountain range enveloped in fog and desert terrain.[/ce_figure]

The bewitchment report

Critics sometimes add the report in Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī 5763 that a man named Labīd ibn al-Aʿṣam worked magic on the Prophet, so that for a time he imagined he had done something he had not done. The same report says that God informed him of the cause, that he was cured, and that the matter concerned ordinary daily affairs. Muslim scholars have long held that it touched nothing of the revelation, which the Quran guarantees. The report presents a prophet who suffered as other human beings suffer, and whom God protected.

What follows

The sources present a man who was frightened by his first experience, who was reassured by those who knew his character best, who grieved when revelation paused, and whose opponents called him mad while his message demanded the very things a demonic influence would oppose. The despair passage that carries the heaviest weight in the critic's case is the one Muslim hadith scholarship itself identifies as disconnected. Read with the same standards that critics apply to Isaiah, Daniel, Moses and Elijah, the first revelation fits what the Quran calls it: the beginning of a burden that the Prophet carried for twenty-three years.

articles.title: Did Muhammad Order the Killing of His Critics?
articles.excerpt: Critics cite Kaʿb ibn al-Ashraf, Asmāʾ bint Marwān and Abū ʿAfak as poets killed for mocking the Prophet. The reports differ sharply in reliability and in what they describe.
articles.content:
Three names recur whenever critics argue that Muhammad silenced his opponents by force: Kaʿb ibn al-Ashraf, Asmāʾ bint Marwān and Abū ʿAfak. All three are described as poets, and all three are said to have been killed at the Prophet's instruction for verses against him. The conclusion drawn is that critics killed on his order prove that Islam punishes criticism with death. The three cases do not stand on the same evidence, and they do not describe the same thing. Treating them as one story hides both facts.

[ce_figure id="pexels-39921634"]Open books with Turkish text arranged neatly under natural light.[/ce_figure]

Two questions that must be kept apart

The first question is historical: did the event happen as reported? Islamic scholarship has its own discipline for answering that, based on the reliability of each chain of narrators, and it applies the discipline to reports that favour the Prophet as strictly as to those that embarrass him. The second question is moral and legal: if the event happened, what was the person killed for? An answer to the first question settles nothing about the second, and an argument that skips from "he was killed" to "he was killed for criticism" has skipped the step that matters.

Asmāʾ bint Marwān and Abū ʿAfak

The stories of Asmāʾ, a woman said to have been killed at night for verses mocking the Muslims, and Abū ʿAfak, an elderly man said to have been killed for similar verses, are the most emotive of the three. They are also the weakest. Neither appears in Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī, Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim or any of the six canonical collections. They come from the biographical literature, chiefly Ibn Isḥāq's biography of the Prophet and the compilation of Ibn Saʿd, whose chain runs through al-Wāqidī, a historian whom the hadith critics rejected as a transmitter.

The version with a full chain fares worse. Ibn ʿAdī recorded it in his catalogue of weak narrators through Muḥammad ibn al-Ḥajjāj al-Lakhmī and noted that the narrators accused this man of forging it. Ibn al-Jawzī listed the report among fabrications, and in the modern period al-Albānī classed it as fabricated (mawḍūʿ). Al-Bukhārī said of Muḥammad ibn al-Ḥajjāj that his narrations are to be rejected. By the standards Muslim scholars apply to every report, these two stories do not establish that the events took place.

Critics sometimes respond that Muslims discard reports only when they are inconvenient. The charge has force only if the standard is applied selectively. Here it is applied consistently: the same scholars who reject the Asmāʾ report also reject fabricated reports praising the Prophet, and the narrators involved were judged weak in every subject they transmitted, not merely in this one.

[ce_figure id="pexels-25588034"]Ancient stone arch ruins with scenic view in Düzce, Türkiye, showcasing classical Roman architecture.[/ce_figure]

Kaʿb ibn al-Ashraf

Kaʿb's case is different, because it is reported in the most authoritative collections. Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī preserves it through Jābir ibn ʿAbd Allāh:

مَنْ لِكَعْبِ بْنِ الأَشْرَفِ فَإِنَّهُ قَدْ آذَى اللَّهَ وَرَسُولَهُ
"Who will deal with Kaʿb ibn al-Ashraf? He has harmed God and His Messenger."
Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī 4037

Muḥammad ibn Maslamah volunteered, and Kaʿb was killed. Any honest account has to accept that this happened and that it happened at the Prophet's instruction. The question is what "harmed God and His Messenger" refers to, and here the biographical sources fill in the context that the hadith compresses.

Kaʿb was a leader of the Banū al-Naḍīr, one of the Jewish tribes of Medina bound to the Muslims by the covenant that governed the city. After the Battle of Badr in 624, according to the early biographers, he travelled to Mecca, mourned the Quraysh dead in verse and urged the Quraysh to take revenge on the Muslims. He returned to Medina and composed verses about Muslim women. The Quraysh were at war with Medina, and within a year they would march on it at Uḥud.

A treaty-bound member of a city's alliance who travels to the enemy's capital in wartime and urges it to attack the city is doing something that every legal tradition, ancient and modern, treats as treason. Poetry was the propaganda of Arabia, the medium through which tribes rallied for war; Kaʿb's verses were part of a campaign of incitement, and that campaign was directed at people who would shortly be killed in battle. One may still judge the method harsh. That is a fair moral discussion. It is a different discussion from the claim that the Prophet killed people for disagreeing with him.

[ce_figure id="pexels-18368859"]Stunning panoramic view of palm trees in an arid desert oasis under a clear blue sky.[/ce_figure]

What the Quran says about mockery

The Quran addresses mockery of the believers and of their faith directly, and its instruction is patience:

۞ لَتُبْلَوُنَّ فِىٓ أَمْوَٰلِكُمْ وَأَنفُسِكُمْ وَلَتَسْمَعُنَّ مِنَ ٱلَّذِينَ أُوتُوا۟ ٱلْكِتَٰبَ مِن قَبْلِكُمْ وَمِنَ ٱلَّذِينَ أَشْرَكُوٓا۟ أَذًۭى كَثِيرًۭا ۚ وَإِن تَصْبِرُوا۟ وَتَتَّقُوا۟ فَإِنَّ ذَٰلِكَ مِنْ عَزْمِ ٱلْأُمُورِ ﴿١٨٦﴾
"You will surely be tested in your possessions and in yourselves. And you will surely hear from those who were given the Scripture before you and from those who associate others with Allah much abuse. But if you are patient and fear Allah - indeed, that is of the matters [worthy] of determination."
Sūrat Āl ʿImrān 3:186

The verse anticipates exactly what the critics describe, hurtful speech from opponents, and its command is endurance and God-consciousness. Elsewhere it tells believers what to do when they hear the verses of God ridiculed:

وَقَدْ نَزَّلَ عَلَيْكُمْ فِى ٱلْكِتَٰبِ أَنْ إِذَا سَمِعْتُمْ ءَايَٰتِ ٱللَّهِ يُكْفَرُ بِهَا وَيُسْتَهْزَأُ بِهَا فَلَا تَقْعُدُوا۟ مَعَهُمْ حَتَّىٰ يَخُوضُوا۟ فِى حَدِيثٍ غَيْرِهِۦٓ ۚ إِنَّكُمْ إِذًۭا مِّثْلُهُمْ ۗ إِنَّ ٱللَّهَ جَامِعُ ٱلْمُنَٰفِقِينَ وَٱلْكَٰفِرِينَ فِى جَهَنَّمَ جَمِيعًا ﴿١٤٠﴾
"And it has already come down to you in the Book that when you hear the verses of Allah [recited], they are denied [by them] and ridiculed; so do not sit with them until they enter into another conversation. Indeed, you would then be like them. Indeed Allah will gather the hypocrites and disbelievers in Hell all together -"
Sūrat al-Nisāʾ 4:140

The instruction is to leave the gathering until the conversation turns to something else. The Prophet lived for years in Mecca among people who mocked him openly, and the sources record no attempt to have any of them killed. When he entered Mecca as its ruler in 630, he pardoned the great majority of those who had fought and ridiculed him for two decades.

What the evidence supports

Set out case by case, the record looks like this. Two of the three famous stories rest on chains that Muslim hadith criticism itself judges fabricated, and they cannot bear the weight placed on them. The third is authentic, and on the account of the early sources it concerns a treaty ally who incited an enemy at war against the city he was bound to protect. None of the three shows a policy of killing people for criticism, and the Quran's own instruction about mockery points the other way.

Modern discussions of blasphemy law in Muslim societies deserve serious attention in their own right, and some of what is done today in the name of honouring the Prophet bears little resemblance to his conduct. That debate is better served by an accurate account of what happened in Medina than by a list of names stripped of their sources and their circumstances.

articles.title: If the Quran Calls Jesus the Word of God, Is He Divine?
articles.excerpt: The Quran calls Jesus a word from God and a spirit from Him. Christian writers read these titles as hints of divinity. The verses that use them say what they mean.
articles.content:
The Quran gives Jesus titles it gives no other prophet. He is al-Masīḥ (the Messiah), a word from God, and a spirit from Him. He is born of a virgin, speaks in the cradle, heals the blind and the leper, and is raised to God. Christian apologists argue that these titles fit the Christian Jesus better than the Muslim one: a being who is the Word of God and God's Spirit, they say, must share in God's nature. The argument deserves a direct answer, and the Quran supplies it in the same verses that contain the titles.

[ce_figure id="pexels-3272118"]Close-up of an ornate Quran page with prayer beads, showcasing Islamic calligraphy and design.[/ce_figure]

The verse that gives both titles

Both phrases appear together in a single verse addressed to the People of the Book. It is the natural place to begin, because the verse itself explains the titles.

يَٰٓأَهْلَ ٱلْكِتَٰبِ لَا تَغْلُوا۟ فِى دِينِكُمْ وَلَا تَقُولُوا۟ عَلَى ٱللَّهِ إِلَّا ٱلْحَقَّ ۚ إِنَّمَا ٱلْمَسِيحُ عِيسَى ٱبْنُ مَرْيَمَ رَسُولُ ٱللَّهِ وَكَلِمَتُهُۥٓ أَلْقَىٰهَآ إِلَىٰ مَرْيَمَ وَرُوحٌۭ مِّنْهُ ۖ فَـَٔامِنُوا۟ بِٱللَّهِ وَرُسُلِهِۦ ۖ وَلَا تَقُولُوا۟ ثَلَٰثَةٌ ۚ ٱنتَهُوا۟ خَيْرًۭا لَّكُمْ ۚ إِنَّمَا ٱللَّهُ إِلَٰهٌۭ وَٰحِدٌۭ ۖ سُبْحَٰنَهُۥٓ أَن يَكُونَ لَهُۥ وَلَدٌۭ ۘ لَّهُۥ مَا فِى ٱلسَّمَٰوَٰتِ وَمَا فِى ٱلْأَرْضِ ۗ وَكَفَىٰ بِٱللَّهِ وَكِيلًۭا ﴿١٧١﴾
"O People of the Scripture, do not commit excess in your religion or say about Allah except the truth. The Messiah, Jesus, the son of Mary, was but a messenger of Allah and His word which He directed to Mary and a soul [created at a command] from Him. So believe in Allah and His messengers. And do not say, "Three"; desist - it is better for you. Indeed, Allah is but one God. Exalted is He above having a son. To Him belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth. And sufficient is Allah as Disposer of affairs."
Sūrat al-Nisāʾ 4:171

The verse calls Jesus a messenger, God's word conveyed to Mary, and a spirit from Him. In the same sentence it forbids excess in religion, forbids saying "three," declares that God is one and is far above having a son, and states that everything in the heavens and the earth belongs to Him. A reading that takes the titles as evidence of divinity has to set aside the rest of the verse that contains them. The verse presents the titles and the denial of divinity together as one statement.

What "a word from Him" means

The phrase kalimah minhu (a word from Him) first appears in the annunciation to Mary.

إِذْ قَالَتِ ٱلْمَلَٰٓئِكَةُ يَٰمَرْيَمُ إِنَّ ٱللَّهَ يُبَشِّرُكِ بِكَلِمَةٍۢ مِّنْهُ ٱسْمُهُ ٱلْمَسِيحُ عِيسَى ٱبْنُ مَرْيَمَ وَجِيهًۭا فِى ٱلدُّنْيَا وَٱلْءَاخِرَةِ وَمِنَ ٱلْمُقَرَّبِينَ ﴿٤٥﴾
"[And mention] when the angels said, "O Mary, indeed Allah gives you good tidings of a word from Him, whose name will be the Messiah, Jesus, the son of Mary - distinguished in this world and the Hereafter and among those brought near [to Allah]."
Sūrat Āl ʿImrān 3:45

Mary asks how she can have a child when no man has touched her, and the angel answers by explaining the mechanism of the word:

قَالَتْ رَبِّ أَنَّىٰ يَكُونُ لِى وَلَدٌۭ وَلَمْ يَمْسَسْنِى بَشَرٌۭ ۖ قَالَ كَذَٰلِكِ ٱللَّهُ يَخْلُقُ مَا يَشَآءُ ۚ إِذَا قَضَىٰٓ أَمْرًۭا فَإِنَّمَا يَقُولُ لَهُۥ كُن فَيَكُونُ ﴿٤٧﴾
"She said, "My Lord, how will I have a child when no man has touched me?" [The angel] said, "Such is Allah; He creates what He wills. When He decrees a matter, He only says to it, 'Be,' and it is."
Sūrat Āl ʿImrān 3:47

The word is God's creative command, "Be." Jesus is called a word from God because he came into being by that command alone, without a father. The Quran draws the comparison explicitly a few verses later:

إِنَّ مَثَلَ عِيسَىٰ عِندَ ٱللَّهِ كَمَثَلِ ءَادَمَ ۖ خَلَقَهُۥ مِن تُرَابٍۢ ثُمَّ قَالَ لَهُۥ كُن فَيَكُونُ ﴿٥٩﴾
"Indeed, the example of Jesus to Allah is like that of Adam. He created Him from dust; then He said to him, "Be," and he was."
Sūrat Āl ʿImrān 3:59

Adam had neither father nor mother and came into being by the same command. If creation by divine command made someone divine, Adam would have the stronger claim. The Quran's point runs the other way: the virgin birth shows God's power to create as He wills, and it places Jesus alongside Adam as a creature brought into being by a word.

This differs from the Logos of John's Gospel, where the Word is with God, is God, and becomes flesh. The Quran uses kalimah for a word God speaks, and in the Quran God speaks many words: the words of God cannot be exhausted though the sea were ink (18:109). Jesus is one such word, uniquely so in the manner of his creation. He is never the eternal speech of God itself.

[ce_figure id="pexels-9820926"]A hillside landscape with olive trees under a soft evening sky, capturing rural tranquility and natural beauty.[/ce_figure]

What "a spirit from Him" means

The second title, rūḥun minhu (a spirit from Him), is read by Christian writers as a reference to the Holy Spirit or to a divine nature. The Arabic preposition min, "from," indicates source and origin, and the Quran uses the same construction for things no one considers divine. It says of everything in the heavens and the earth that it is "all from Him":

وَسَخَّرَ لَكُم مَّا فِى ٱلسَّمَٰوَٰتِ وَمَا فِى ٱلْأَرْضِ جَمِيعًۭا مِّنْهُ ۚ إِنَّ فِى ذَٰلِكَ لَءَايَٰتٍۢ لِّقَوْمٍۢ يَتَفَكَّرُونَ ﴿١٣﴾
"And He has subjected to you whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth - all from Him. Indeed in that are signs for a people who give thought."
Sūrat al-Jāthiyah 45:13

And it uses the language of God's spirit for the creation of every human being, beginning with Adam:

ثُمَّ سَوَّىٰهُ وَنَفَخَ فِيهِ مِن رُّوحِهِۦ ۖ وَجَعَلَ لَكُمُ ٱلسَّمْعَ وَٱلْأَبْصَٰرَ وَٱلْأَفْـِٔدَةَ ۚ قَلِيلًۭا مَّا تَشْكُرُونَ ﴿٩﴾
"Then He proportioned him and breathed into him from His [created] soul and made for you hearing and vision and hearts; little are you grateful."
Sūrat al-Sajdah 32:9

A spirit "from God" is a spirit God created and sent. The phrase honours Jesus by attributing his life directly to God's act, as Adam's life was. It does not make him a part of God, any more than the heavens and the earth become divine by being "from Him."

[ce_figure id="pexels-39392696"]Serene cloudscape with sunlight rays piercing through dramatic clouds.[/ce_figure]

How Jesus describes himself in the Quran

The Quran also reports Jesus's own words, and his first recorded speech, spoken as an infant in the cradle, is a statement of identity:

قَالَ إِنِّى عَبْدُ ٱللَّهِ ءَاتَىٰنِىَ ٱلْكِتَٰبَ وَجَعَلَنِى نَبِيًّۭا ﴿٣٠﴾
"[Jesus] said, "Indeed, I am the servant of Allah. He has given me the Scripture and made me a prophet."
Sūrat Maryam 19:30

His self-description is servant and prophet. When the Quran later summarises his status, it adds a detail that answers the divinity claim with a plain physical fact:

مَّا ٱلْمَسِيحُ ٱبْنُ مَرْيَمَ إِلَّا رَسُولٌۭ قَدْ خَلَتْ مِن قَبْلِهِ ٱلرُّسُلُ وَأُمُّهُۥ صِدِّيقَةٌۭ ۖ كَانَا يَأْكُلَانِ ٱلطَّعَامَ ۗ ٱنظُرْ كَيْفَ نُبَيِّنُ لَهُمُ ٱلْءَايَٰتِ ثُمَّ ٱنظُرْ أَنَّىٰ يُؤْفَكُونَ ﴿٧٥﴾
"The Messiah, son of Mary, was not but a messenger; [other] messengers have passed on before him. And his mother was a supporter of truth. They both used to eat food. Look how We make clear to them the signs; then look how they are deluded."
Sūrat al-Māʾidah 5:75

The verse notes that Jesus and his mother both ate food. A being who needs to eat depends on what God created to sustain him. The Quran asks its readers to look at what dependence implies.

Honour without divinity

The Christian argument assumes that the most exalted titles must point to divinity, because a mere human being could not deserve them. The Quran works with a different assumption: God can honour a creature to the highest degree without the creature ceasing to be a creature. Abraham is the friend of God, Moses is the one to whom God spoke directly, Muhammad is the seal of the prophets, and Jesus is the word and spirit from God, the Messiah, born of a virgin and raised to Him. Each title marks a particular favour. None of them crosses the line between Creator and creation, which is the line the Quran guards above all others.

Christians and Muslims therefore agree on more about Jesus than either side often admits: his virgin birth, his miracles, his status as Messiah, his return. They disagree about what those facts mean. The Quran's titles cannot settle that disagreement in favour of divinity, because the verses that give the titles are the same verses that deny it. A reader who wants to argue for the Trinity must make the case from other sources. The Quran will not supply it.

articles.title: Is Muhammad Foretold in the Bible?
articles.excerpt: Muslims point to Deuteronomy 18 and the Paraclete of John as prophecies of Muhammad. Christians reply that both point elsewhere. An honest weighing of the texts.
articles.content:
The case for Muhammad in the Bible begins with the Quran, which says that the Jews and Christians find the Prophet described in the Torah and the Gospel. Muslim writers have long pointed to two passages in particular: the promise in Deuteronomy of a prophet like Moses, and the promise in John's Gospel of a Paraclete, a helper or comforter, who would come after Jesus. Christian writers reply that the first prophecy points to an Israelite and the second to the Holy Spirit. Both sides often argue past each other. This article sets out the texts, states the strongest case on each side, and asks what the Quran's claim depends on.

[ce_figure id="pexels-11716937"]Flat lay of vintage paper with ink bottle and pen on a colorful wooden surface.[/ce_figure]

The Quran's claim

ٱلَّذِينَ يَتَّبِعُونَ ٱلرَّسُولَ ٱلنَّبِىَّ ٱلْأُمِّىَّ ٱلَّذِى يَجِدُونَهُۥ مَكْتُوبًا عِندَهُمْ فِى ٱلتَّوْرَىٰةِ وَٱلْإِنجِيلِ يَأْمُرُهُم بِٱلْمَعْرُوفِ وَيَنْهَىٰهُمْ عَنِ ٱلْمُنكَرِ وَيُحِلُّ لَهُمُ ٱلطَّيِّبَٰتِ وَيُحَرِّمُ عَلَيْهِمُ ٱلْخَبَٰٓئِثَ وَيَضَعُ عَنْهُمْ إِصْرَهُمْ وَٱلْأَغْلَٰلَ ٱلَّتِى كَانَتْ عَلَيْهِمْ ۚ فَٱلَّذِينَ ءَامَنُوا۟ بِهِۦ وَعَزَّرُوهُ وَنَصَرُوهُ وَٱتَّبَعُوا۟ ٱلنُّورَ ٱلَّذِىٓ أُنزِلَ مَعَهُۥٓ ۙ أُو۟لَٰٓئِكَ هُمُ ٱلْمُفْلِحُونَ ﴿١٥٧﴾
"Those who follow the Messenger, the unlettered prophet, whom they find written in what they have of the Torah and the Gospel, who enjoins upon them what is right and forbids them what is wrong and makes lawful for them the good things and prohibits for them the evil and relieves them of their burden and the shackles which were upon them. So they who have believed in him, honored him, supported him and followed the light which was sent down with him - it is those who will be the successful."
Sūrat al-Aʿrāf 7:157
وَإِذْ قَالَ عِيسَى ٱبْنُ مَرْيَمَ يَٰبَنِىٓ إِسْرَٰٓءِيلَ إِنِّى رَسُولُ ٱللَّهِ إِلَيْكُم مُّصَدِّقًۭا لِّمَا بَيْنَ يَدَىَّ مِنَ ٱلتَّوْرَىٰةِ وَمُبَشِّرًۢا بِرَسُولٍۢ يَأْتِى مِنۢ بَعْدِى ٱسْمُهُۥٓ أَحْمَدُ ۖ فَلَمَّا جَآءَهُم بِٱلْبَيِّنَٰتِ قَالُوا۟ هَٰذَا سِحْرٌۭ مُّبِينٌۭ ﴿٦﴾
"And [mention] when Jesus, the son of Mary, said, "O children of Israel, indeed I am the messenger of Allah to you confirming what came before me of the Torah and bringing good tidings of a messenger to come after me, whose name is Ahmad." But when he came to them with clear evidences, they said, "This is obvious magic.""
Sūrat al-Ṣaff 61:6

Two claims are made here. The first is that the earlier scriptures contain a description of the Prophet that their readers would recognise. The second is that Jesus announced a messenger to come after him, whose name is Aḥmad, a form from the same root as Muhammad meaning "most praised." Neither verse cites a chapter and verse, and the Quran elsewhere holds that the earlier scriptures, as transmitted, contain both genuine revelation and human alteration. The Quran's claim therefore does not stand or fall with any single passage in the present Bible.

Deuteronomy 18: a prophet like Moses

Moses tells Israel that God will raise up a prophet like him.

"I will raise them up a Prophet from among their brethren, like unto thee, and will put my words in his mouth; and he shall speak unto them all that I shall command him."

Deuteronomy 18:18 (King James Version)

The Muslim reading notes three features. The prophet is "from among their brethren," and the Hebrew Bible uses "brethren" for related nations as well as for fellow Israelites; Moses calls the Edomites, the descendants of Esau, Israel's brethren:

"And command thou the people, saying, Ye are to pass through the coast of your brethren the children of Esau, which dwell in Seir; and they shall be afraid of you: take ye good heed unto yourselves therefore:"

Deuteronomy 2:4 (King James Version)

The descendants of Ishmael, Abraham's other son, stand in the same relation. Second, God will put His words in the prophet's mouth, which matches the Quran's account of revelation as words delivered to an unlettered prophet who repeats them. Third, the prophet is like Moses: a lawgiver who led a community, fought its battles, governed it and left a scripture. Muslims argue that Muhammad fits that profile more closely than Jesus, who brought no new law and held no political rule. The closing chapter of Deuteronomy adds that no prophet like Moses arose afterwards in Israel:

"And there arose not a prophet since in Israel like unto Moses, whom the LORD knew face to face,"

Deuteronomy 34:10 (King James Version)

The Christian reply has real weight, and an honest treatment must state it. Three verses earlier, the same promise reads "from the midst of thee, of thy brethren":

"The LORD thy God will raise up unto thee a Prophet from the midst of thee, of thy brethren, like unto me; unto him ye shall hearken;"

Deuteronomy 18:15 (King James Version)

"From the midst of thee" most naturally means from within Israel. The New Testament applies the prophecy to Jesus in Peter's sermon in Acts 3:22. And Deuteronomy 34:10, written as a retrospective, can be read as saying that no such prophet had arisen by the time of writing, which leaves the identity open.

Weighed fairly, Deuteronomy 18 is a contested text. The Muslim reading is possible, and the "like Moses" criterion favours it; the Christian reading is also possible, and the phrase "from the midst of thee" favours it. Neither side can claim a decisive proof from these verses alone.

John's Paraclete

In John's Gospel Jesus promises his disciples another helper.

"And I will pray the Father, and he shall give you another Comforter, that he may abide with you for ever;"

John 14:16 (King James Version)

"Nevertheless I tell you the truth; It is expedient for you that I go away: for if I go not away, the Comforter will not come unto you; but if I depart, I will send him unto you."

John 16:7 (King James Version)

Muslim writers make several points. The helper comes only after Jesus departs; he is "another" helper, which implies a figure distinct from Jesus and comparable to him; he will guide into all truth and will not speak of himself, only what he hears, which recalls the Quran's description of a prophet who speaks only what is revealed to him. Some have argued that the Greek paraklētos replaced an original periklytos, "renowned," close in meaning to Aḥmad. No surviving manuscript has periklytos, and that particular argument is speculation.

The Christian reply is again direct. John identifies the helper by name a few verses later:

"But the Comforter, which is the Holy Ghost, whom the Father will send in my name, he shall teach you all things, and bring all things to your remembrance, whatsoever I have said unto you."

John 14:26 (King James Version)

The helper is to be with the disciples for ever and to dwell in them, which describes an indwelling spirit more naturally than a human prophet born six centuries later. Muslims who take the Paraclete as Muhammad must hold that the identification with the Holy Spirit is a later layer in the text, and that claim needs evidence that has not been produced.

The honest assessment is that John 14 to 16 offers Muslims less than Deuteronomy 18. The features that echo the Quranic Prophet are real, and the passage's own identification points elsewhere.

What the Quran's claim depends on

Popular Muslim apologetics has sometimes overstated these texts, presenting them as proofs that any fair reader must accept. The texts do not support that confidence, and overstating them does the case no service. The Quran's own claim is more modest and harder to dismiss: that the earlier scriptures, before and during their transmission, carried expectations of a prophet to come, and that some among the Jews and Christians of Arabia recognised the description. The early sources record such recognitions, from Waraqah ibn Nawfal in Mecca to the Christian king of Abyssinia.

For a reader deciding between Islam and Christianity, the decisive evidence lies elsewhere: in the Quran itself, its preservation, its account of God, and the life of the man who delivered it. Prophecy texts can show that a claim is consistent with earlier scripture. They cannot show by themselves that it is true, and on these two passages the most that either side can fairly say is that the reading is disputed.
